extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent drafters, and patent examiners working under the European Patent Convention (EPO practice); attendees of US Bar – EPO liaison
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examination principles for drafting and interpreting claims under Article 84 EPC (clarity, conciseness, support) and their interplay with other EPC requirements (novelty, inventive step, sufficiency). Aimed at ensuring claims define protection clearly and are commensurate with the technical contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 84 EPC — Claims must define, be clear, concise, supported
rubrics_metrics.description: "The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. They shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description." (Art. 84 EPC; Rule 43 EPC; Guidelines F-IV 4–6)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must meet form and content requirements (Rule 43) and the Guidelines sections on clarity, conciseness and support (F‑IV,4; F‑IV,5; F‑IV,6). This is the primary legal requirement for claim drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity from the claim wording alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of the terms of the claim should be clear for the person skilled in the art from the wording of the claim alone, without reference to the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited sources: T 2/80; GL F‑IV, 4.1 and 4.2. Examiner/expert should not have to rely on the description to make the claim intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should be read to make technical sense (with good will) and be contradiction‑free
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should be read with an attempt to make technical sense out of it (with good will), and the claims must be free of contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive principle to give reasonable technical meaning where possible, but not at the expense of creating contradictions or ambiguity in claim terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 69 EPC and Protocol — interpretation limits
rubrics_metrics.description: "The extent of the protection conferred... shall be determined by the claims. Nevertheless, the description and drawings shall be used to interpret the claims." (Art.69(1) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art.69 and its Protocol do not allow excluding what is literally covered by claim terms or reading limitations from the description into the claims to avoid novelty/inventive step objections. A claim must be clear on its own (GL F‑IV,4.2; T 223/05; T 681/01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional features — when allowable
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional features are allowable if they provide a clear instruction to a skilled person to reduce them to practice without undue burden and cannot otherwise be defined more precisely without restricting scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law examples: T 1048/10 (allowable), T 979/11 (clarity — no), T 68/85; T 1098/14 (allowable example wording such as 'suitable for conforming...'). Use functional language only where it gives sufficient teaching to implement the feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of vague/relative terms unless well‑recognised in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative terms should not be used unless they have a well‑recognised meaning in the particular art and that is the intended meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unclear term cannot be allowed in a claim if the term is essential given the invention. Examples: 'substantially non‑polymerisable' (T 445/12 — clarity no) vs 'middle polyhedron' (T 610/13 — clarity yes because well‑recognised in mathematics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must include essential features underlying technical effect (Art.84 vs Art.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: If features in a claim do not achieve the necessary technical effects underlying the solution of the objective technical problem, the claim may lack inventive step (Art.56) and/or lack clarity because it omits essential features (Art.84).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: GL F‑IV, 4.5.1. A claim that omits features presented in the description as essential may be unsupported even if it appears broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination approach: derive missing features from description or raise inventive‑step objection
rubrics_metrics.description: In examination, if the examiner can derive from the description the remaining features needed to carry out the invention, an objection that an essential feature is missing (Art.84) will be raised; if not, an objection of lack of inventive step (Art.56) will be raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examination workflow for deciding whether the defect is a clarity/support issue or an inventive‑step/novelty issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency (Art.83) vs clarity (Art.84) — scope vs teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Art.83 is fulfilled if the application contains sufficient information to allow the person skilled in the art to perform the invention over the whole area claimed without undue burden; Art.84 is fulfilled if the skilled person can, from the application as filed, extend the particular teaching to the whole of the field claimed using routine methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References: GL F‑III,1 and GL F‑IV,6.3. Distinguishes the threshold for sufficiency (enablement) from the requirement that claim breadth be commensurate with the teaching in the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art.83 and Art.84 can give rise to simultaneous objections
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim, over its whole range, extends to technical subject‑matter not made available to the skilled person by the application as filed, objections may be raised under both Art.83 and Art.84; both objections could be raised at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GL F‑IV,6.4. Examiners may raise both lack of sufficiency and lack of clarity/support when claim scope is not commensurate with the disclosed teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (Art.54) vs clarity (Art.84) — broad claims problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The broader a claim, the easier it is that the claim is not new (Art.54) or not supported by the description (Art.84). Very broad claims are normally both not new and not supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner will choose to raise a novelty or clarity objection depending on which is more efficient for concluding examination. Practical note on prosecution strategy and claim breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and compliance with Rule 43 (form and content of claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be concise (Guidelines F‑IV,5) and comply with the form and content requirements of Rule 43 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness is a separate formal/content requirement in addition to clarity and support; ensure claim wording avoids unnecessary verbosity and complies with prescribed claim structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy rationale — clarity reduces uncertainty and delimitation disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear claims reduce the 'area of uncertainty' between prior art, alleged infringing subject‑matter, and the invention — i.e., 'good fences make good neighbours.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical justification for strict clarity/support standards: precise claim borders reduce borderline infringement issues and litigation/administrative uncertainty.
